newsitem.title: USA: U.S. issues rule on "fresh" poultry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. issues rule on "fresh" poultry.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department said Tuesday that -- in time for Christmas dinner next year -- store-bought poultry can carry the label "fresh" only if the birds have never been cooled below 26 F.
In final rules published in the Federal Register, the department said poultry chilled below 26 F but above zero will not be required to bear any specific fresh/frozen label.
But, from December 1997, poultry cooled at or below zero will be labeled "frozen" or "previously frozen."
This is the second go-around for the department, which issued a final rule on poultry labeling in August 1995, which was overriden by Congress this summer.
Originally, the department had sought to bill poultry cooled to less than 26 F but not below zero as "hard chilled" or "previously hard chilled."
Lawmakers have wrangled for the past few years over what can be sold as "fresh," which commonly fetches a higher price in grocery stores than frozen.

Consumer advocates, who see the dispute as a truth in labeling issue, once staged a "bowling for broilers" stunt on Capitol Hill using rock-hard poultry as bowling balls to show that "fresh" could be icy under the existing rules.
